title: Cloud Essentials
subtitle: Climb the money ladder — one cloud question per grade level

questions.q: Which of the following BEST describes cloud computing?
options: A private server locked in your office closet
On-demand computing resources delivered over the internet with pay-as-you-go pricing
A USB drive you carry with you to store files
Software that only runs on mainframe computers
questions.note: Cloud computing is on-demand delivery of IT resources over the internet. You pay only for what you use, just like a utility bill.

explain.correct: Cloud computing means accessing compute, storage, and services on demand over the internet and paying only for what you consume — no large upfront hardware purchase required.
wrong: A private on-premises server is not cloud computing; it lacks on-demand self-service and internet delivery.
A USB drive is local physical storage, not a networked computing resource delivered on demand.
Cloud services run on distributed commodity hardware in provider data centers, not exclusively on mainframes.

questions.q: Which THREE companies are known as the 'big three' public cloud providers?
options: Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud Platform
IBM Cloud, Oracle Cloud, and Salesforce
questions.note: AWS, Azure, and GCP dominate the global cloud market. CompTIA Cloud+ expects you to recognize all three by name and core brand.

explain.correct: Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud Platform (GCP) are the three largest public cloud providers by revenue and market share.
wrong: IBM Cloud and Oracle Cloud are real providers but are not the dominant 'big three'; Salesforce is a SaaS vendor, not an IaaS/PaaS platform.
Netflix, Spotify, and Dropbox are cloud-based consumer services — they are CUSTOMERS of cloud providers, not providers themselves.
Dell, HP, and Lenovo are hardware manufacturers, not public cloud platform providers.

questions.q: A company subscribes to Microsoft 365 for email and Office apps. Which cloud service model does this represent?
questions.note: SaaS delivers a fully managed application over the internet. The provider handles everything from hardware to the app itself; the customer just uses it.

explain.correct: Microsoft 365 is a complete, ready-to-use application suite delivered over the internet — the textbook definition of SaaS. The provider manages the OS, runtime, middleware, and application.
wrong: IaaS provides raw virtual machines, networking, and storage (e.g., Amazon EC2). The customer manages the OS and everything above it.
PaaS provides a managed development platform and services like databases (e.g., Azure App Service, Google App Engine). The customer manages their application code.
DaaS delivers a virtual desktop environment; Microsoft 365 is a productivity application suite, not a virtual desktop.

questions.q: A hospital runs sensitive patient records on its own data-center hardware while also using AWS for its public website. Which cloud deployment model does this describe?
questions.note: Hybrid cloud combines a private environment (on-premises or dedicated) with one or more public clouds, connected by a network link.

explain.correct: Hybrid cloud blends private and public cloud resources. Here the hospital keeps regulated patient data on private infrastructure while offloading the public website to AWS.
wrong: Public cloud means all resources are owned and operated by a third-party provider and shared among tenants — the hospital's private servers are not public cloud.
Private cloud means all resources are dedicated to a single organization. Using AWS for the website adds a public cloud component, making it hybrid.
Community cloud is shared among organizations with a common mission (e.g., government agencies) — this scenario involves one private org plus a public provider.

questions.q: A developer needs to store billions of images accessible via HTTP URL, with no fixed size limit. Which storage type is the best fit, and which AWS service represents it?
questions.note: Object storage treats each file as a discrete object with metadata and a unique URL. It scales to virtually unlimited capacity and is accessed over HTTP/HTTPS.

explain.correct: Object storage (Amazon S3) stores data as individual objects retrievable via HTTP URL with flat namespace and unlimited scale — ideal for images, videos, and static assets.
wrong: Block storage (Amazon EBS) presents raw block devices for use by a single EC2 instance, typically for OS volumes or databases. It does not scale to billions of objects and is not accessed via URL.
File storage (Amazon EFS) provides a shared POSIX filesystem mounted by multiple instances — useful for shared config or home directories, not individual URL-addressable media objects.

Amazon Glacier (S3 Glacier) is archive-tier object storage designed for infrequent access; retrieval takes minutes to hours and it is the cheapest tier. The developer needs fast HTTP access, not archive retrieval.

questions.q: Under the AWS Shared Responsibility Model, which of the following is ALWAYS the customer's responsibility regardless of the service model (IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS)?
options: Physical security of the data center hardware
The data the customer stores in the cloud
Maintaining the global network fiber infrastructure
questions.note: No matter the service model, the customer owns and is responsible for their own data — classification, protection, and access controls to that data always belong to the customer.

explain.correct: Data is always the customer's responsibility. The provider never takes ownership of customer data regardless of whether the service is IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS.
wrong: Physical security of data center hardware (locks, guards, cameras, environmental controls) is always the cloud provider's responsibility under all service models.
The hypervisor is part of the cloud provider's core virtualization infrastructure; patching it is always the provider's responsibility.
Global network fiber and backbone infrastructure is owned and maintained by the cloud provider, not the customer.

questions.q: An admin requires all users to enter a password AND approve a smartphone push notification before accessing the cloud console. Data traveling between the browser and the cloud is encrypted. Which TWO security controls are in use?
options: Multi-factor authentication (MFA) and TLS encryption in transit
Biometric authentication and encryption at rest (SSE)
Role-based access control (RBAC) and VPN tunneling
questions.note: MFA combines something you know (password) with something you have (phone). TLS (Transport Layer Security) encrypts data moving between endpoints — this is encryption in transit.

explain.correct: Password + smartphone push = two distinct factors, which is MFA. Browser-to-cloud encryption uses TLS (HTTPS), which is encryption in transit — both are foundational cloud security controls.
wrong: Single-factor means only one authentication factor (e.g., password only). IPsec encrypts network-layer tunnels, not browser-to-application HTTPS sessions.
Biometric authentication is not mentioned; SSE (server-side encryption at rest) encrypts stored data, not data in transit between browser and cloud.
RBAC controls what authenticated users are authorized to do; VPN provides encrypted network tunnels. Neither describes the password+push MFA combination or standard HTTPS TLS in this scenario.

questions.q: A DevOps team uses a single set of configuration files to provision identical infrastructure on both AWS and Azure. The same tool also works with Google Cloud. Which tool and category BEST match this use case?
options: AWS CloudFormation — cloud-specific Infrastructure as Code
questions.note: Terraform by HashiCorp uses declarative HCL files and provider plugins to manage infrastructure across AWS, Azure, GCP, and hundreds of other platforms from a single workflow.

explain.correct: Terraform is the leading multi-cloud IaC tool. Its provider model lets one codebase provision and manage resources on AWS, Azure, GCP, and beyond using declarative configuration files.
wrong: AWS CloudFormation is also IaC but is AWS-only — it cannot provision Azure or GCP resources.
Kubernetes orchestrates containerized workloads and manages their lifecycle (scheduling, scaling, healing). It does not provision cloud infrastructure like VMs, networks, or storage accounts.
AWS Lambda is a serverless compute service that runs event-driven functions. It does not provision or manage infrastructure across cloud providers.

questions.q: On Sunday a FULL backup runs. Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday each run an INCREMENTAL backup. To restore the system to its Wednesday state, which backups must you apply?
options: Sunday full + Monday + Tuesday + Wednesday incrementals, applied in order
Any single incremental, since each one contains the full dataset
questions.note: An incremental backup stores only the changes since the LAST backup of any kind. Restoring requires the full backup PLUS every incremental in unbroken sequence up to the target point — one missing or corrupt incremental breaks the chain. (This is the trade-off vs a differential, which needs only the full + the latest differential.)

explain.correct: Each incremental holds only the delta since the previous backup, so restoring Wednesday's state needs the Sunday full plus the Monday, Tuesday, AND Wednesday incrementals applied in order.
wrong: Skipping Monday and Tuesday loses their changes — Wednesday's incremental only holds the delta since Tuesday, not the whole week. You need the full, unbroken chain.
A single incremental holds only one period's changes, not the full dataset — you must start from the full backup and replay every incremental.
Incrementals are deltas, not full copies; no single incremental can rebuild the whole system on its own.

questions.q: A financial services company needs near-zero recovery time and is willing to pay maximum cost. A startup with a tight budget can tolerate hours of downtime after a disaster. Which DR strategies BEST match each scenario, in that order?
options: Pilot light for the financial firm; active-active for the startup
Active-active for the financial firm; backup-and-restore for the startup
Warm standby for the financial firm; pilot light for the startup
Backup-and-restore for the financial firm; active-active for the startup
questions.note: Active-active runs full duplicate environments simultaneously for near-zero RTO at maximum cost. Backup-and-restore is the cheapest strategy with the highest RTO — acceptable only when hours of downtime are tolerable.

explain.correct: Active-active keeps identical live environments running in parallel across regions; failover is instant (near-zero RTO) but doubles infrastructure cost. Backup-and-restore stores data in cheap storage and restores from scratch after a disaster — lowest cost but RTO measured in hours.
wrong: Pilot light keeps only a minimal core running (e.g., a replicated database) and scales up after disaster — RTO is minutes to an hour, not near-zero. Active-active for the startup would be unnecessarily expensive for a budget-constrained organization tolerating hours of downtime.

Warm standby keeps a scaled-down version of the full environment running; failover is fast (minutes) but not near-zero RTO and is less expensive than active-active. Pilot light for the startup is more expensive than backup-and-restore and not the best fit for an hours-tolerant budget scenario.

Backup-and-restore for a zero-RTO financial firm is the worst possible DR choice — restoring from backup takes hours. Active-active for a budget-limited startup is the most expensive strategy available.

questions.q: A company is moving a legacy web app to AWS with NO code changes, just copying it to an EC2 instance. They also plan to run batch processing jobs that can be interrupted. Which migration strategy and pricing model apply, in that order?
questions.note: Rehost (lift-and-shift) moves a workload to cloud with zero code changes. Spot Instances offer up to 90% discount over On-Demand but can be interrupted — ideal for fault-tolerant batch jobs.

explain.correct: Rehost copies the app as-is to EC2 — the first of the 6 R's migration strategies, requiring no code modifications. Spot Instances let AWS reclaim capacity with a 2-minute warning; the steep discount makes them ideal for interruptible batch workloads.
wrong: Replatform makes minor cloud-optimized changes (e.g., switching to a managed database) without full rearchitecting. Reserved Instances require a 1- or 3-year commitment and suit steady, predictable workloads, not interruptible batch jobs.

Refactor (re-architect) means redesigning the application to be cloud-native (e.g., microservices, serverless) — the most expensive and time-consuming migration path, not applicable to a no-code-change move. On-Demand is flexible but carries the highest per-hour price.

Repurchase (drop-and-shop) means replacing the application entirely with a SaaS product (e.g., moving from a custom CRM to Salesforce) — not applicable when migrating existing code to EC2. Savings Plans provide flexible commitment discounts for compute usage, not the optimal choice for interruptible batch processing.
